findings.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default (evaluated once at import time), not a `default_factory`, so every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` shares one stale process-startup timestamp — any future ordering/race-resolution logic layered on this field would silently misbehave

src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:16 — queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default evaluated once at module-import time, not per-instance, so every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` (including all instances from `from_integration`) shares the identical stale timestamp instead of the actual creation time; should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)

src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:33 — from_dict` performs no runtime type validation, so a JSON round-tripped payload with `queued` as an ISO string (or any other type) is silently accepted into a field typed `datetime`, leaving the object in an inconsistent state if `queued` is ever relied upon later

src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:35 — to_dict()` uses `asdict()` which leaves the `queued` field as a raw `datetime` object; when `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes this dict as Celery task kwargs (`sync.py:143`), the default JSON task serializer cannot encode a `datetime`, so `apply_async` will raise at enqueue time (or silently coerce/fail depending on broker config), meaning every outbound sync carrying an assignment_source could fail to be scheduled at all.

src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:17 — queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition/import time (a classic mutable-default-style dataclass pitfall), so every `AssignmentSource` created without explicitly passing `queued` shares the same stale timestamp for the life of the process rather than reflecting when it was actually constructed.

tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:29 — test_to_dict only asserts result.get("queued") is not None, so it would still pass if `queued` were a stale shared class-level default (real risk since `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class-definition time as a mutable dataclass field default) rather than a fresh per-instance timestamp; test never instantiates two AssignmentSource objects to compare queued values or checks freshness against the current time.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:33 — from_dict` performs no runtime type validation, so a JSON round-tripped payload with `queued` as an ISO string (or any other type) is silently accepted into a field typed `datetime`, leaving the object in an inconsistent state if `queued` is ever relied upon later

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource.from_dict`, the code simply does `return cls(**input_dict)` and only guards against `ValueError`/`TypeError`. Since Python/dataclasses don’t enforce type annotations at runtime, a payload with `queued` set to a string (e.g., after JSON serialization) would be accepted and stored in the `queued: datetime` field without parsing/validation. In this diff, current logic only uses `integration_id` for cycle prevention, so it’s not a demonstrated correctness failure yet, but it is a real robustness/consistency issue introduced by the new `AssignmentSource` round-trip path.

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` the dataclass field is defined as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. The correct pattern would be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to capture creation time per instance.

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` (new file `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`), the dataclass field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` at class-definition/import time, so every instance that doesn’t explicitly pass `queued` will share the same (stale) timestamp. This is a real correctness bug; it should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The finding’s note about the test (`test_to_dict` only asserting non-None) is accurate and would not catch the shared-default issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:1 — No test exercises AssignmentSource.from_dict round-tripping through actual JSON serialization (e.g. json.loads(json.dumps(source.to_dict()))), which is what really happens when assignment_source_dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg; datetime is not JSON-serializable by default so a real bug in that path would go undetected.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which includes the `queued: datetime` field (see `assignment_source.py`). That dict is passed directly into a Celery task kwarg (`sync_group_assignee_outbound` -> `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(... assignment_source_dict=assignment_source.to_dict() ...)`). If the task serializer is JSON (a common/default Celery setup), a `datetime` value is not JSON-serializable, so this can break the outbound sync at runtime. The new tests only assert `queued` exists in the dict and never exercise the actual (de)serialization boundary implied by `apply_async`, so this potential defect would not be caught.
